extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; practicing scientists and advanced students interested in the history and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for diagnosing normal science, scientific revolutions, and theory choice—how communities evaluate theories, judge scientific progress, and decide between competing paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm (priority of paradigms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms are universally recognized scientific achievements that, for a time, provide model problems and solutions to a community of practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms serve as exemplars that define legitimate problems and methods, shape professional education, and provide the conceptual boxes into which normal research fits. They may coexist rarely; possession of a paradigm is a key condition for the developmental transition Kuhn describes. Examples: Newtonian mechanics, Lavoisier's chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science (research predicated on paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science is the activity predicated on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like; it is largely puzzle-solving conducted within the paradigm’s commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science is strenuous, devoted, often suppresses fundamental novelties (because they subvert basic commitments), and relies on the conceptual boxes provided by professional education. Its success and direction derive from the educationally instantiated commitments of the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzle-solving ability (dominant selection criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demonstrated ability to set up and to solve puzzles presented by nature is the dominant criterion by which scientific communities judge theories and practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When values conflict in theory-choice, puzzle-solving effectiveness usually prevails. This includes producing concrete research results and solving the range of problems the community faces; it explains why later theories are judged better in practice even without a theory-independent notion of 'truth'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of prediction (especially quantitative prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy of prediction—particularly quantitative prediction—is a primary and useful criterion for distinguishing better from earlier theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn lists this explicitly among the most useful criteria for comparing theories and for establishing that later theories are better instruments for puzzle-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of different problems solved
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the number of distinct problems a theory successfully solves, the stronger its claim as an improved scientific theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count of problems solved serves as a concrete measure of a theory’s fruitfulness and practical superiority in puzzle-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between esoteric and everyday subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance a theory strikes between esoteric (specialized) and everyday (ordinary) subject matter is a criterion for evaluating its usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn lists this as one of the useful criteria for distinguishing earlier from later theories—how widely and practically applicable the theory’s problem-solving reach is matters to communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, scope, and compatibility with other specialties
rubrics_metrics.description: Values such as simplicity, broad scope, and compatibility with other specialties are important but, Kuhn argues, less decisive than predictive accuracy and problem-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features influence theory appraisal but are not always sufficient to determine choice between incompatible theories; they are supplementary values communities consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomaly resolution and crisis (triggering revolutionary change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent, unresolvable anomalies—failures of normal problems to yield expected results or apparatus to behave as anticipated—attract attention and can induce crisis, a precondition for revolutionary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When anomalies cannot be aligned with professional expectation despite repeated efforts, normal science goes into crisis and extraordinary investigations begin; such crises open the possibility for new paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary change (incompatibility and standards shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific revolution involves the rejection of a time-honored scientific theory in favor of an incompatible alternative that shifts the problems available for scrutiny and the standards for what counts as admissible problems and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions transform the scientific imagination and the world within which work is done; they are characterized by incompatibility, reconstruction of prior theory, re-evaluation of prior facts, and changes to problem and standard-setting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and conversion (mechanisms of persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For one scientific community to accept another’s viewpoint requires translation (rendering results and arguments into mutually intelligible terms) and, ultimately, conversion (an internalized gestalt-like shift into the new language/worldview).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation alone is often insufficient; persuasion typically requires concrete research results that are describable in shared terms and the longer process of translation that generates more such results. Conversion is not a mere rational choice but a cognitive/sociological shift; it often occurs gradually and involuntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook tradition and invisibility of revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks present the finished achievements of science and thereby tend to obscure or render invisible the historical process and the revolutionary breaks that produced current paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because textbooks are pedagogic and persuasive, they mask the actual processes of theory change; this is why revolutions have been difficult to see from within the received literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological insufficiency (limits of method alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological directives and textbook-depicted methods are insufficient to dictate unique substantive scientific conclusions; prior experience, accidental choices, and individual/historical contingencies play formative roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple incompatible conclusions can be scientifically legitimate given observation and method; what differentiates competing schools is their incommensurable ways of seeing and practicing science, not simple methodological failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational embedding / socialization (community formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm’s answers become firmly embedded through professional education and socialization, licensing students for practice and creating rigidities that direct normal research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure of education and community membership (who is admitted, how they are trained) is crucial to how paradigms persist, how normal science proceeds, and how conversions and revolutions spread; community characteristics thus function as evaluative and enabling criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress criteria distinct from ontological 'truth'
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific progress is best judged by improvements in problem-solving, prediction accuracy, scope, and related practical values rather than by a theory-independent approximation to 'what nature is really like.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that later theories are 'better' instruments for solving puzzles even if there is no coherent, theory-independent notion that later ontologies are closer to reality; lists of pragmatic criteria can reliably distinguish earlier from later theories.
